w4-meaning~idea.cta: What a suffix means on the Word road
w4-meaning~idea.title: What a suffix means
w4-meaning~idea.body: A suffix sits at the END of a word. "-less" means without: fearless is without fear. "-ful" means full of. A suffix often changes the word's job too — "kind" describes, "kindness" is a thing.
w4-meaning~idea.more: I can say what a common suffix means.

li4-theme~idea.cta: What is it really about? on the Literature road
li4-theme~idea.title: What is it really about?
li4-theme~idea.body: The plot is what happens; the theme is what the story is really ABOUT, the big idea underneath. A fable often states its lesson as a moral: "Plodding wins the race". The theme is that steady effort beats careless talent. To find a theme, ask: what does the main character learn, or what would the writer like us to think about?
li4-theme~idea.more: I can say what a story is really about.

author~shakespeare.title: William Shakespeare
author~shakespeare.body: Written about 1595–96, first printed 1600; Shakespeare died 1616.
author~shakespeare.more: Their books in the Library: A Midsummer Night's Dream · Macbeth · Julius Caesar · Shakespeare's Sonnets.

author~wordsworth.title: William Wordsworth
author~wordsworth.more: Their books in the Library: Poems, in Two Volumes.

why~sonnets.title: Why read Shakespeare's Sonnets?
why~sonnets.body: 154 fourteen-line poems about love, time and beauty, including the most famous poem in English.
why~sonnets.more: Told in the Library: “Sonnet 18: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?” · “Sonnet 116: Let me not to the marriage of true minds”.

why~blake.title: Why read Songs of Innocence and of Experience?
why~blake.body: Pairs of simple-sounding poems, such as The Lamb and The Tyger, that ask very big questions.
why~blake.more: Told in the Library: “The Lamb” · “The Tiger” · “Holy Thursday (Songs of Experience)”.
why~blake.cta: Songs of Innocence and of Experience in the Library

why~wordsworth.title: Why read Poems, in Two Volumes?
why~wordsworth.body: Home of "I wandered lonely as a cloud": nature remembered and treasured.
why~wordsworth.more: Told in the Library: “I wandered lonely as a Cloud” · “The Solitary Reaper”.
why~wordsworth.cta: Poems, in Two Volumes in the Library

why~keats.title: Why read Poems (1817)?
why~keats.body: Keats's first book, with his sonnet on discovering Homer.
why~keats.more: Told in the Library: “On the Grasshopper and Cricket” · “On first looking into Chapman's Homer”.

why~mariner.title: Why read The Rime of the Ancient Mariner?
why~mariner.body: A ghostly sea ballad about a sailor who shoots an albatross.
why~mariner.more: Told in the Library: “Water, water, every where”.
why~mariner.cta: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner in the Library

why~dickinson.title: Why read Poems: Three Series?
why~dickinson.body: Short, surprising poems with dashes and slant rhymes, unlike anything before them.
why~dickinson.cta: Poems: Three Series in the Library

why~lear.title: Why read A Book of Nonsense?
why~lear.body: The book that made the limerick famous.
why~lear.cta: A Book of Nonsense in the Library

why~garden-verses.title: Why read A Child's Garden of Verses?
why~garden-verses.body: Poems written as a child sees things: shadows, swings, bedtime and rain.
why~garden-verses.more: Told in the Library: “My Shadow” · “The Swing” · “The Land of Counterpane”.
why~garden-verses.cta: A Child's Garden of Verses in the Library

why~gitanjali.title: Why read Gitanjali (Song Offerings)?
why~gitanjali.body: The book of prayer-poems that made Tagore the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
why~gitanjali.more: Told in the Library: “Where the mind is without fear”.

why~crescentmoon.title: Why read The Crescent Moon?
why~crescentmoon.body: Tagore's poems about childhood, often in a child's own voice.
why~crescentmoon.more: Told in the Library: “The Champa Flower”.
why~crescentmoon.cta: The Crescent Moon in the Library

why~naidu.title: Why read The Golden Threshold?
why~naidu.body: Musical poems of Indian life by the poet called "the Nightingale of India".
why~naidu.cta: The Golden Threshold in the Library
